transcript: It's funny that one of the best plays I've seen about AI was actually written ten years ago. Making a very timely Broadway debut, Marjorie Prime by Jordan Harrison is still futuristic but strikingly resonant. It opens with 85-year-old Marjorie speaking with a significantly younger man. We come to learn this is her husband, and then we come to learn this is an artificial representation of her husband, who is deceased. For Marjorie, whose memory is fading, the AI provides on-demand companionship and clarity, as her daughter and son in law have fed it information. Though the technology is advanced, it can still only learn based on what it's told, which as shown in the play, makes it possible to rewrite history or omit memories intentionally. Thematically speaking, the play is not really about AI, it's about grief. But in showing how these characters work through their grief with technology, it questions what that says about our ability to connect with each other in reality and in life. It's kind of heartbreaking, kind of funny, and kind of eerie, all in one. June Squibb brings a playful and somewhat mischievous energy to Marjorie, perfectly complimented by Danny Burstein's earnest and sincere portrayal of her son-in-law. Something worth noting is that when a character is written to be in their 80s, it's not uncommon to cast someone who's a bit younger than that, since 80s is well into retirement territory. But at 96 years old, June Squibb is even older than the character she's playing, which is an amazing feat and must be some kind of record. You can find her, Danny Burstein, Cynthia Nixon, and Michael Lowell at the Hayes on Broadway through February 15th. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
